notes.meaning: Nathan respectfully asked David if the king had secretly chosen a new ruler without telling his trusted advisers. Nathan knew God had promised the throne to Solomon, so he wanted David to clear up the confusion.
David called Bathsheba back into the royal chamber. She had stepped out while Nathan spoke with the king, following proper court manners. Now the king was ready to give his decision.

David made a solemn vow in the name of the living Lord, who had rescued him from every trouble. He promised Bathsheba that he would place Solomon on the throne that very day, just as he had earlier sworn. Remembering God's past faithfulness gave the dying king strength to do what was right.
Bathsheba bowed low to the ground to show deep honor and thanks to David. She prayed that the king would live forever, showing she truly cared for him and was not merely greedy for power.
David summoned Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the military commander. These were faithful men who had refused to join Adonijah's rebellion.

The king ordered his leaders to place Solomon on David's own royal mule and take him down to the spring of Gihon. In those days, letting someone ride the king's personal mule was a clear sign that he was the chosen royal successor. Gihon was an open, public place near Jerusalem where the crowds could easily see what was happening.

Zadok and Nathan were instructed to pour sacred oil on Solomon to make him king, while the people blew trumpets and shouted praises. Then Solomon was to sit on David's throne to rule the nation at once. This public ceremony showed everyone that Solomon ruled with the full blessing of God and King David.

Benaiah answered "Amen," asking God to confirm the king's decision. He prayed that the Lord would stay with Solomon and make his kingdom even greater than David's. David was glad to hear this prayer, because a loving father desires his children to do even better than himself.
Zadok, Nathan, Benaiah, and the royal bodyguards quickly carried out the king's orders. They placed Solomon on David's mule and brought him down to Gihon.

Zadok took a horn filled with holy oil from the sacred tent and anointed Solomon as king. The priests blew the ram's horn, and all the people shouted, "Long live King Solomon!" The sacred oil showed that God had chosen Solomon and would give him the strength to rule well.

A massive crowd followed Solomon back into the city, playing flutes and shouting with joy. The celebration was so loud that the ground seemed to shake beneath their feet. God's people were overjoyed to welcome the leader David had appointed.
Adonijah and his guests heard the loud blast of the ram's horn just as their feast was ending. Joab, the veteran army general, heard the noise and wondered why the city was in such an uproar.
While Joab was speaking, Jonathan the son of Abiathar the priest arrived at the banquet. Adonijah welcomed him warmly, assuming that such a worthy man must be bringing good news.

Jonathan broke the bad news that David had officially crowned Solomon. He explained that Zadok and Nathan had anointed Solomon at Gihon, escorted by the royal guard. The loud noise ringing through the valley was the entire city rejoicing over the true king.
Jonathan also reported that Solomon had already taken his seat on the royal throne. Solomon was no longer just an heir waiting for the future, but was actively ruling as king right then.

The royal officers went to King David's bedside to congratulate him and bless Solomon's name. David bowed in worship on his bed, praising the Lord for letting him live to see his son placed on the throne. The aged king gave all the credit to God for keeping His promise.
Panic swept through the banquet as soon as Adonijah's guests heard Jonathan's report. The plot collapsed instantly, and every guest ran away to save his own life.

Adonijah was terrified of King Solomon, so he ran to the altar and grasped its four raised corners, called horns. In Israel, taking hold of the altar was a plea for mercy, asking God and the king to spare one's life.
Messengers told Solomon that Adonijah was clinging to the altar in great fear. Adonijah asked the new king to make a formal promise not to put him to death with the sword.

Solomon granted Adonijah conditional mercy. If Adonijah showed himself to be an honorable man, not a hair on his head would be harmed, but if he acted wickedly or plotted rebellion again, he would die.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars translate the condition as showing himself to be a loyal subject rather than a traitor, seeing it primarily as a demand for political loyalty.

notes.meaning: Solomon sent guards to bring Adonijah down from the altar. Adonijah came and bowed low before Solomon, accepting him as his ruler, and Solomon told him to return to his own house and live quietly.
